utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-14/2-T. The Prosecutor versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next exhibit, please, Mr. Cicak, is exhibit 64. In fact, it's 64/1, 64/1(a), because it was not included in the compiled bundle or the original list of exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Cicak, this is another article published by you on the 27th of March in the newspaper, I think Nasa Rijec, and it was headed as "Sancta Simplicitus Kordicu" and there is an English summary of the article. Again, if you're familiar with the article or if you have a chance to scan it briefly now to remind yourself of what it contains, I will read to the Court the English summary, 64/1(a), which is to the following effect; the text is in the form of a letter to Kordic by yourself, summarised as: "Kordic's version of neo-fascism has all the hallmarks of true fascism; a national party is the main government of authority; power in the hands of the leader; a personality cult of the irreplaceable national leader with transformation of democratic government into fascist government. "Kordic has been arming the semi-military HDZ army, indoctrinating the young and assisted by Stipac, Sliskovic, Prusak. Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina have been led to believe that they should be Ustashas in order to be Croats, which is ridiculous. "All proposals made by people from other parties, non-HDZ people, have been marginalised purely because they come from the other. The HDZ structure has developed into a corrupt, harmful, extremist, warmongering organisation. "Slogans like, 'This is NDH, the Independent State of Croatia,' are meant to convince people that Busovaca has negligible Muslim and Serbian population. Busovaca is Bosnia and it will never be Croatia. "Thanks to Kordic and Boban, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna is a political cancer on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the only thing they have to offer the population of Busovaca is war as a way of life." Mr. Cicak, does that summary cover some of the topics covered in the article "Sancta Simplicitas"?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: To put it briefly, this is really just a summary of an article that belongs to an anthology. It was written about Mr. Kordic, and it contains everything that Mr. Kordic carries in himself, everything negative. And he was really among the foremost, as far as these negative things are concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Cicak, can I put your mind at rest to this extent? Although this article has been summarised at the moment for the Court, full translations of this article and, indeed, of all the articles will be available for the Court to read in due course. So with those comments by you on this article, I want to move to the next exhibit, Exhibit 52.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: I would just like to ask you the following: Could we just comment on this a bit more, with the permission of the Honourable Court?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If there are particular matters that you don't think are covered in the summary I've read out and that you -- just before we hand out the next exhibit -- you think there are matters that aren't covered in the summary, and in particular if you can point to the numbered paragraph numbers on the original 64/1, that would help us. Where we can't read BCS, we can see the paragraph numbers on our photocopies of the document you have. Are there any particular numbered paragraphs you want to draw to the Court's attention?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: I would like to draw the Court's attention to the following. This text, "Sancta Implicitas" written to Kordic did not come into being just like that. It was in response to a very confusing article that was written by Mr. Kordic, himself. It was called "Cicak Small-Time Judas." I think you have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We're coming to that.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think you have that among your documents. No, no, no. These two documents have to be looked at together.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to come to the "Small-Time Judas" next, and would it be convenient if we reserved any other comments you have on this article until after we've looked at that article?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: Just the way you want it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. This article, which was published at about this time,"Cicak Mali Juda", we have fully translated, and I shall read the full translation. Just to be quite sure, there have been two translations of this document, I think, over time, this one is in four sheets, and the fourth sheet has heavily stamped over it "Draft Translation". I trust that's the copy that the Court has.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So this article, published in March of 1992, in the Lasva Herald, reads as follows: "According to the law on publishing, we are availing ourselves of the right to use some of the BH /Bosnia-Herzegovina/ press space to show the unscrupulous and wild campaign against Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina by quasi-Croats who have become permanently blinded by Yugoslav or union-oriented Bosniak Cause. "We have no intention of getting angry or feeling hurt that the well-known enemies of the policy which would resolve the global Croatian issue are relentlessly attacking the people, and the policy that has, at its core, the interest of Croats in Herceg-Bosna. They cannot reconcile themselves to the fact that Croats of Herceg-Bosna are no longer the amorphous mass they were for a long time but a sovereign people on a national sovereign territory. Union-supporters and federalists of all kinds are terrified by the prospect of Croats using the HDZ in Bosnia-Herzegovina /Croatian Democratic Union in Bosnia and Herzegovina/ which forms part of a unique HDZ, to achieve the objective, which we were unable to do in BH, even after multi-party elections in 1990, that is, the complete and absolute sovereignty of the Croatian people which is what is owed to them as one of the three constituent peoples in BH."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The Prosecutor please read a bit slower for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: "The BH HDZ held its Central Board Meeting in Livno in the presence of about 140 of the most prominent and legitimate officials of the Croatian people, (presidents of HDZ municipal boards from the whole BH, representatives in the BH Assembly, members of the BH HDZ Main Board and Presidency, the presidents of the SO /Municipal Assembly/, and the IO SO /Executive Board of the Municipal Assembly/ nominated by the HDZ, members of the Presidency and the Government from the ranks of the HDZ). With merely four abstaining votes, they confirmed the full unity of the Croatian people built on the Croatian experience in BH. Therefore, the electorate placed its complete trust in these Croats belonging to the HDZ to lead the Croatian people in BH in the right direction, and not in some quasi-Croatian intellectuals from civic parties or sick blabbermouths such as the weak-spirited Dragutin CICAK, the tool and the sacrificial lamb of the KOS-like /Counter-Intelligence Service/ unity-supporting Bosniak association. "Let us remind the ill-informed attackers and the wild assailants targeting Croatian rights that the European Community/EC/ through Mr. Cutilierro, asserted that the path cleared by the HDZ, by us, was the best and that it was the right one. "Therefore, we say yes to external borders for BH, but we also yes to an internal structure consisting of national units (cantons) with the full sovereignty of the three peoples. Gentlemen, the BH HDZ has actually respected European standards, whereas the Balkan Bosniak bullies, such as comrade Cicak or comrade Nikola Pisker tend to behave like bulls in a china shop. "Therefore, whether we call these national units pens, cages or whatever you like, they are, dear comrades, the reality of European politics, which everyone will agree with, because that is the only way not to have the referendum results annulled, that is, not to have a savage war break out between the peoples of BH. The HDZ has shown its support for a unified BH with the mass response of Croats to the referendum, but at the same time, they let everybody know that, without a fair agreement of the three peoples, there can be no peace in BH. "Unfortunately, BH media RTV radio and television, free Bosnia, or more adequately (RTV/Radio and Television/, Oslobodenje, Slobodna Bosna/Free Bosnia/ (or more adequately union-prone Bosnia)..." and then another title in the same batch as the others, "... led the campaign of vilification against the Croatian people and the Croatian policy as implemented by the HDZ in BH. They are only interested in having large numbers of pamphlets against the Croatian people and Croatian policies published among readers' letters to editors, as has been done in the past ten days or so by the mentally unbalanced comrade Dragutin Cicak. The weekend visitor from Zenica, an alien body infiltrated in Busovaca, managed to get the post of the vice-president of the Busovaca HDZ municipal board. However, he could not completely suppress his destructive alcoholic spirit and it floated up to the surface showing Comrade Cicak as a person who had to retire because of alcoholism, had his driving license permanently revoked because of the same reason and registered by the police as a person who, while in a fit, killed his neighbour's chained watchdogs. "By changing his place of residence Comrade Cicak obviously thought he could bury his past. Not so. The Busovaca HDZ has recently managed to acquire confirmed information about Mr. Cicak's work for the enemy, the present republic media, that is everything but Croat. "Therefore, gentlemen from the press and the RTV and the other so-called Croatian intellectuals, do not let yourselves be laughed at by the public and accept the fact (as well as the right to be beaten which you may not express/as printed/) that the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna is an expression of the will of the vast majority of the Croatian people, as are all other Croatian communities, and that as such it has already become part of the structure of BH under the auspices of the EC, which has been working in an unbiased and objective manner - to us the only judge we will listen to. Cease further vilification of Mr. Mate Boban and other leaders of the Croatian people, who are legitimate representatives of the Croatian peoples. It is obvious that Europe is not negotiating with Cicak, Komsic, Mikulic or Lovrenovic who only represent themselves, as they have a right to. "Avoid ridicule and cease your attacks against Dr. Franjo Tudjman, the President of the Croatian State recognised by the civilised world, the State that uses implacable democratic methods to pave the way in order to improve the life of all citizens of the Republic of Croatia. "P.S. "As far as we are concerned, this is our final response and we do not want to enter into any polemics or correspondence with persons who are not worth the paper, who advertise false peacemaking which contributed to the destruction of Ravno and other Croatian villages. "Comrade Cicak, you no longer have the right to sign your name as the vice-president of the Busovaca HDZ, because you were unanimously removed from that function in the presence of 30 representatives, at the session of the Busovaca HDZ municipal board on 9 March 1992. Cicak's hunger for the top posts - that also escaped him the HKD/expansion unknown/Napredak branch and the Busovaca HDZ - was finally dispersed with the irrevocable procedure of his expulsion from HDZ membership." And then that document comes from the Busovaca HDZ municipal board, president, Dario Kordic. Mr. Cicak, first of all, the English translation that I've been reading, does that accord with the contents of the document? Just yes or no, and correct anything that's significantly wrong.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. A matter of detail before we pass from it. On the very last paragraph, there were some initials that the interpreter was unable to expand, and can you help at all with what is described as HKD? Can you help us with what HKD was, if you know?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: The Croatian cultural society of Napredak.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Coming in the English version to the penultimate sheet, sheet 3, and finding the place in the article where the allegations were made against you, to the paragraph that begins "unfortunately, BH media," in that paragraph, things are said about you including that you were a weekend visitor from Zenica. Can you explain what, if anything, underlies that allegation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know what that allegation is supposed to mean. Comrade Kordic should know that. My registered place of residence is in the town of Busovaca, where I lived, in that village of mine, just like all other citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It then makes reference to alcoholism and to losing your driving license because of drink. Had you in fact lost your driving license?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: My driver's license was never taken away, and as far as drinking is concerned, I can just state that light cola is a great drink.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Finally, there is an allegation about killing a neighbour's dogs. What about that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: I have no idea what Comrade Kordic had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next paragraph but one after that contains in brackets a phrase, which those who wish to can see in originals on the right hand of the three columns of the article and about eight lines down, a phrase which says "as well as the right be beaten, which you may not express." And this may or may not be a question for you or for the interpreters, but the word "beaten," to what type of beating does that word refer?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: It refers to that kind of physical destruction of a man that leads to his death.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, this article, in the copy we have, is not specific as to its date. From your previous answers, is it your recollection that that article preceded "Sancta Simplicitas"?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It was published in a few different information media. I don't know when the Lasvanski Glasnik was first published and I'm not really interested in that. Before that, it was carried in some other media in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. The Court will appreciate that its original number, 52, was too early in the chronology of events because that would be right at the beginning of the month. It's probably best left with its number and we just have to acknowledge that it has a date that falls on this witness's evidence before exhibit 64/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Cicak you said when you wanted to make some further comments about your article "Sancta Simplicitas" that it needed to be seen beside the article "Cicak Mali Yuda." Can we now turn to 64/1, "Sancta Simplicitas," and can you tell us, please, what comments it is that you feel have to be made to amplify the article, bearing in mind the real need to deal with matters succinctly in the interests of getting your evidence to a conclusion quite swiftly.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: I shall try to do that in a few sentences. Several dozen articles that I had to present in public because I could not struggle against Kordic through regular democratic channels, through the HDZ, so this was carried in the media. "Sancta Simplicitas" is in response to "Small Time Judas," which is a very confusing article. However, it did merit an answer, because "Cicak, Small Time Judas," is an article that addresses me personally, Comrade Kordic addresses me personally, and he presents all kinds of nonsense in this article. In my article, "Sancta Simplicitas," I ask him to answer my people, the Bosnian Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and tell them what he has done to them and what he will do to them. That's what I wanted. It's not that he has to answer to me; there was no need for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: After the publishing of your article on the 27th of March, and before something happened that happened on the 30th of March, did you receive any warning of what was coming -- going to happen?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know what warning have you in mind, from the HDZ authorities, or the citizens who live in the town of Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: From any individual.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, some individuals told me that something was in the making, and that it did not augur well, and that I should take care of myself, of my life.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who were the individuals who gave you that warning?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: My barber first and foremost, where I went regularly for haircuts and shaves, and various other individuals, prominent citizens of Busovaca, including the director of a factory in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Any warning from anybody close to the HDZ or part of the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. The loudest, the most vociferous, was Mr. Anto Stipac. He even refused to be on speaking terms with me any more, and he opposed the contents of all that I wrote.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's come to what happened to you. On the 30th of March of 1992, had you gone out in the course of the day?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At approximately what time did you return?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: I went out around 8.00 in the morning, I think it was Monday, as I had promised the editor of Slobodna Bosna that I would contribute a special article for him, so I wrote that article and mailed it, and between 8.00 in the morning until 2.00 in the afternoon, I was in the town of Busovaca, and then I went home.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you got back home, did you notice anything that was out of place or unusual?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. That is, the place where I live, where my property is, is very tame, people are very forthcoming, and I was -- on my property I felt like everybody else, like all the other citizens of the world, I had my pets, I had a dog and I had a cat, and when they would see me a few hundred metres away from my home, they would greet me. That day, when I was coming home to the village around 14.00, there was nobody to be around, not a single villager, and there was not a sound. One could hear a fly moving through the air. I mean, an incredible silence had descended on the village. At first I paid no attention to it. Then, since my dog did not greet me, and he would always greet me, I became suspicious: Why was all that happening? And only as I came near my house I realised what the problem was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What was the problem, and what happened next?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: The problem was that I was moving towards the entrance door, it is a huge oak wood door, and I saw that it was ajar. And all of a sudden, from the passage, that is, from the inside, the door suddenly burst open. Three uniformed men rushed out. The first one was Marko Kulic, nicknamed Zelenika. He ran into me, hit me with his fist forcefully in the face, so that my lips were bleeding, my nose was bleeding, and if we are sitting as we were standing, like that, at that time, from the right-hand side, two other men rushed out and from the left-hand side another one. They were all armed. They pounced upon me. They were all over me, and they simply lifted me in the air and took me into the house. And as soon as I entered the anteroom and the living room, I saw that everything had been demolished, that everything had been broken, that they had already been inside, so this was an ambush to meet me, and it was several hours earlier in my house -- that is, on my property -- and I could not have known that. Then they put me -- that is, they wouldn't allow me to sit down. They put me on the sofa. To the left was -- I really have no other word for it except the criminal that is Zoran Marinic, nicknamed Svabo. To the right was a young man from Kacuni, and he was known because he had only two front teeth. I do not really know whether it's proper for me to say, but when he laughed, he looked like Dracula. In front was Marko Kulic. The others were breaking things around the house, looking for something, I don't know what. At 14.00, Zoran Marinic, Svabo, had a huge handle, axe handle in his hands, and that young man from Kacuni had a rolling pin, but merely for decorative purposes, I mean that thick, a very long one. And between 2.00 and 4.00 in the afternoon, they began beating my body. That is, they would -- the one to the right would ask me a question, and I would naturally turn to face him and at that moment, Zoran Marinic from my left would hit me for all he was worth, so that I would lose my breath. Then Zoran would ask a question, and I would automatically turn to face him, and then the other one would hit me from the right. And so they alternated between 2.00 and 4.00, beating me systematically. Needless to say, Marko Kulic was helping them, but I was busy with either the left one or the right one, thug, he would then hit me in the stomach.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When they were asking you questions, what sort of things were they saying to you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: All sorts of rubbish. To begin with, it is a very degrading event when you are battered like that, I think one never recovers fully from it. And what they are telling you beggars the imagination. They asked me what intelligence service I was working for, whether it was KOS, and who was my connection there, who was the KOS man in Busovaca who I was co-operating in KOS, and so on and so forth. Then what were the grudges I bore against Kordic and Boban. Marinic, particularly really took it out on me whenever he would hit me, forcefully, so that I would start gasping for breath and even lose my consciousness for a while, he would say "this is from Dario. This is from Dario, because you keep attacking him. This is for Dario." And I remembered it, and I don't think I will ever forget that. So it was horrible -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When this beating ended, what did these men do? Did they leave the property, or did they leave the property with items? What happened?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: To begin with, they wanted me to write something. I was not in a normal state of mind, I was shaking all over, I was bleeding, my back -- at the back, at the mouth, and so on and so forth. They wanted me to write a statement and I don't know, I can't remember what about, but I think it involved some cooperation with KOS, with KOS, and at that moment I wrote that I cooperated with the CIA, with Mossad, with FBI, with Sigurimi, with SIS, I mean, I wrote down all they wanted. They told me two copies, I don't know if I managed to write it in two copies, because my hands were badly beaten. I couldn't even hold the pencil. But it was one copy or two copies, but had they asked me at that particular moment if I was a member of a group of, I don't know, Saint Peter's or whatever I would have said yes, of course I'm a collaborator. And I do not really want anyone to go through such horrible things. As for the things they took away, that is curious. Your Honours, I should simply like to tell you this, I mean, it should be a political attempt against a man who happens hold a different opinion from the group. That is, if one cannot remedy that through a dialogue, then one resorts to extreme force, because this is a man which bothers the group. But now look at the group. My property was full of everything, that group looted all from the house, they took away money, gold, I mean, whatever they laid their hands on. But the funniest, or perhaps the most tragic, the saddest thing is, that that fighting fist directly commanded by Dario Kordic, that is the one which performed the most difficult tasks in this area, those people took from my freezer I don't know how the interpreters will translate it, you know, the refrigerator, they took some beverage, they took all other useful things that were there, and so on and so forth. So it was a bunch of criminals of the lowest dregs that had been recruited for an elite political party.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: To bring this to a conclusion, tell us about the condition of your dog, in a sentence, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that hurt me most, and I'm really sorry for that kind of expression that I use but I can't call him anything else. I call him a little Dracula, because when he had only two teeth in his head. And at some point he took out a knife and wanted to butcher my dog so I said "why don't you slit my throat but leave the dog alone. What's the dog done to you? If I have some reckoning with Dario Kordic --"

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did he do anything to the dog?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: He wanted to slit its throat, but the dog was already lying down helpless because Zoran Marinic had beaten it so badly because Zoran Marinic had to go by the dog to the shed to get that handle with which he would beat me for two hours, and on his way back of course the dog attacked him, and he destroyed the dog completely, I mean, it survived, but it was not a living being any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. In the course of this attack, did your neighbours make themselves known at all, or not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: Absolutely not. It was a show of force. They arrived to the village two hours earlier, and wearing camouflage uniforms, with the latest arms. There was different green, brown, greyish black and so on and so forth, but they all war a disgraceful insignia that is the historical disgrace of Croatia meaning "U." "U" means Ustasha during the fascist regime. Ante Pavelic and others, it epitomised a special military organisation so they wore that insignia and they had the latest weapons. Even to see a young man carrying an M-16 rifle that is an American rifle which had just been used I think in Vietnam --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, before you conclude with that, I would like to find out whether the witness was beaten with anything other than the fists of the attackers? Was he beaten with an implement or implements?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think he told us, but we will just get him to confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you attacked with an implement or implements, and can you just tell Judge Robinson what implement or implements were used.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: Only with implements, but at the entrance, as I was entering my house, that was when Marko Kulic hit me for all he was worth, and I fell to the ground, and that was the only time, but the rest of the time between 2.00 and 4.00, they were beating me with poles, or rather they were not beating me they were battering me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, you've told us about the rolling pin and you've described the implement that was obtained from your garden. Just show us, please, how long was the implement that was used that had come from your own garden?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, the handle, the axe handle, well, it's about one metre 30.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I trust that helps the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, you've told us that your neighbours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Nice, only to complete for the Chamber, we heard the witness speak about KOS, when he was accused of working for KOS. Could we know what KOS stands for?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just help us with that, Mr. Cicak. KOS stand for what?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't really know what that is, but that word kept cropping up, time and time again, in relation to the Yugoslav People's Army. So it is with the Yugoslav People's Army, it was associated, the word "KOS" was associated with the Yugoslav People's Army. But what "KOS" means, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll possibly obtain a formal terminology for that at the short adjournment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you would, Mr. Nice, and I'm sure you're moving on to deal with that, if we could hear about his injuries.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes certainly, I've got two consequential topics, and the witness can hear how I'm going to deal with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's right, isn't it, Mr. Cicak, that you went and saw Kordic did next day and that you also made a complaint to the police and were examined by the police?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you go to the police first, or did you go to Kordic first?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: Kordic first.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let us deal with the Kordic visit first, and then we'll go to the police station and deal with the injuries, because he was indeed photographed, although the photograph isn't very helpful. Mr. Cicak, if we deal, first of all, with the visit to Kordic. The next day, you went to where in order to see the first defendant?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: The next day -- or rather I must say this first. After 4.00, when they stopped beating me, battering me, I laid down completely immobile on the couch until the morning, which was also broken down. I could not sleep, but I just lay down and did not move at all and thought about what had happened to me and how to save my body and myself. As soon as the day broke, -- and of course I could not wash myself, or shave, or get ready. Around 8.00, I went down to Busovaca. I knew that Kordic was in his office, and immediately and highly indignant, I went to him. I was wearing a jacket. It's sort of one of those fashionable materials, I think it's jeans or something like that it is called, and blood seeped through it and came down my fingers. The haematoma, that is, the bruises came -- what's it called? What is this called? Hand, hand. I mean the fist. And so I reached Kordic in this shape, and I asked him, "Dario, are you now happy with what you did?" And he was sitting at his desk and did not reply. I think he tried to say something but did not say it aloud, and I said it was really sad and really disgraceful that when one does not have an argument for a political dialogue, that one then proceeds to beating one, that is, completely destroying a man. And then I undressed and showed him my back, showed Kordic my back and my arms, and this is this photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You have the photograph with you, which is better than the copy we have because it's been photocopied. Can you, first of all, put it on or get the usher to put it on the ELMO and see if it shows up satisfactorily?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know if you can see that. I see nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've got nothing on our monitor. It may be simplest if the document was handed out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Can that be handed first to the Court, then to the Defence counsel?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: May we know when this was taken, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Cicak, when was this photograph taken, to your recollection?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was taken two days later, on the 1st of April. If I may add something. May I? I would like to say something. May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: Have a look at my left arm. That is a haematoma. It was not covered with something, it is a haematoma, and my back was just as black. But as this was done with a flash -- you know, I mean the photograph was taken with a flash, so what you call -- so this is not as black as it was. But on my right hand and on my left arm, one could see the haematoma. And I think that this bruise persisted for more than half a year, perhaps even for a year. And I cannot really use, properly, my hands anymore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Show it to Counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Nice, could we know who took that photograph, and what is the caption below the photograph? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May I have a look at it very briefly myself, and then I'll hand it back to the witness? Yes. Can you hand it to the witness?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: May I say?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you would read out the caption, first of all, the interpreters will do it for us.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: It says, below the photograph, "Cicak beaten and robbed."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And who took the photograph? Was it a newspaper person or someone else?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: A professional journalist for Nasa Rijec. His name is Hakija. I don't know. I know it was taken on the 1st of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I come to exhibiting the original of that photograph, newspaper photograph, or possibly not, at a later stage when we see a copy of it, which may be sufficient for the Court's needs?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, could we return to the visit that he paid the defendant Kordic?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: He asked him if he was not happy with what he had done, and it wasn't clear to me whether Kordic made any reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I will expand on that. There's a little bit more to it, but we interrupted the evidence because he told us of showing his injuries to Kordic, and that's why the photograph was helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You told us, Mr. Cicak, about showing your injuries to the defendant, undressing. Did he say anything to you about knowledge of or involvement in the attack on you or not? What was the position?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: Kordic was never a brave man to tell one, face to face, what he thought about him. And I was very indignant then, and I demanded that I be returned what I had planted. And can you imagine it? You get home. You are met there by armed men. They beat you, and then they rob you. I did not have my wallet with me. I had nothing. I told Kordic, "Please, I want that my wallet or money be returned within half an hour, and all the rest that was looted." Then I left his office and I went to an adjacent office, that is, an office where my enterprise once was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: By that stage, had Kordic said anything to you, one way or another, as to whether he knew anything of this attack or not? Had he stated his position at all, so far as you can recall?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: That position was reflected in that Kordic thought that I would arrive there repenting, as penitent, as somebody who was guilty of something, rather that I would come to show him what he had done and that I would ask him to return what had been taken away from me, what had been -- what I had been robbed of is not so important, but the important thing is that a political dialogue may not end as it did, because it is incompatible with a democratic society. And I also showed him that. Was that what he wanted?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What Judge Robinson wants to know, and perhaps the rest of the Court, is whether he said anything, one way or another, that indicated that he was involved in this or not.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: It is my deep conviction that he just said one sentence. He thought that I would come to see him repentant rather than rebellious. And whether he gave orders to have this done or not is something that I'm not going to say a word about, because I'm sure that the Honourable Judges will ask me about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, Mr. Cicak, the question is, "What did he say that morning when you went to see him?"

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: What I told you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry, we haven't followed that at all. What were his words? Can you just repeat what it was that he said?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: He said exactly the following, that he thought that I would come to him repentant rather than rebellious, and I would like this to be interpreted very accurately.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You went to your office. How near to or far from his office was that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: That's not my office. That is an office belonging to a company that I used to work for before, and that's where my friends worked, and it was about 50 metres away from his office.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What did you next hear of Kordic in relation to all this? Did you make contact with him by telephone?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. When 30 minutes had gone by, I called Kordic and I asked him whether he managed to get all the money. Of course, I didn't have a thing. I didn't have any money, I didn't even have my personal documents. It was very difficult for me to go back, to go to Zenica, but I did it at my own risk. He said, once again, that he had not done it. However, when he took up the receiver and when he talked to me on the phone, because it's a small room, I could feel that there were several persons in that room. Since one man has a very characteristic voice, I can say for sure that this was Mr. Anto Stipac. How Anto Stipac came to Kordic's, who invited him, when, that I do not know. But as I was talking to Kordic, I could feel this argument taking place in the office, so there were several persons in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How does Anto Stipac fit, if at all, in connection with the people at the attack, or Kordic himself, or anyone else? How is he potentially significant?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: Do you want me to give you a comprehensive answer about the entire group or just him?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just a summary. Does he fit in somewhere in this grouping of people?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, he does fit into this group of people, as one of the masterminds of this attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you asked Kordic for your property or money, what was his response?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: That he didn't have it yet and that he still hadn't gotten all the people who had beaten me up together.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you ever get your money back?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you ever get your money or other property back, that which had been taken in the assault at your house?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours. Is this some kind of a joke or what? Is this some kind of humour?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm simply asking you, for the purposes of the evidence, whether your request to Kordic to get your property back was successful or not.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: But no. Whatever they loot, they never return to anyone. That's why I'm asking whether this is some kind of a joke or some kind of a humouristic thing. If it's humour, if it's a joke, then I accept it, but I can't accept it as a serious question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: After your phone call to Kordic, did you leave the office and, in due course, go to the police station?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you go to the local police station or somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not go to the local police station because I did not trust the police, because the local police was destroyed through the activity of Kordic and Mr. Sliskovic. I went to the police station in Zenica --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: -- that was in charge of all crimes, grave crimes on the territory of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Exhibit 65, please. Again, not in the core bundle.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you make a report to the police, of which you have the version in BCS? We have an English translation. I'm going to deal with some of the paragraphs in detail and some of them in summary. It says that the report was prepared on the 1st of April at midday. It sets out who was present, gives your name and address. It sets out the terms upon which you were making your report and says that on the 30th of March, at about 14.00, going home, you noticed the door to your house was open. You thought your daughter was back, and I'm now summarising. Six men with long-barrelled weapons, black suits. The next paragraph, "I can say I know all of them because they are members of the HDZ, of which I am the deputy president. I know two by their names," and you set them out. "The others were also from Busovaca and are members of the paramilitary formation of the HDZ reserve service of Herceg-Bosna." You then make reference to Kordic, Sliskovic and Prusac. "When they came to me, one of them hit me in the face with his fist. Then they dragged me into the house. I noticed that the house had been demolished, certain parts of the furniture cut with a knife, bottles and drink thrown about and opened. They put me on a sofa and started hitting and questioning me." And you set out the questions, "Who are you working for?" a question about KOS. "They warned me that they would turn me into concrete, that is, threatened to kill me, if I reported what was happening. I can say that when they beat me, that is, one of the guys who had a beard beat me with an axe handle over the back and other parts of the body. The other beat me with a pole we used as a rolling pin and had hanging on the wall." You set out how the beating went on until 4.00 and how they left with 5.000 dinars from your wallet and some other items. You say this: "At one moment, Marko Kulic took out a pistol and fired it next to my head as a threat that he would kill me." Is that something that happened or not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Carry on.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: It wasn't only a demonstration with firearms. The young man from Kacuni, whom I call by the silly name of Dracula, he kept sharpening his knife all the time. He was using some kind of a device to do it, and he kept playing with this knife around my throat, my neck. He kept saying, "I'm going to slit your throat right now so that you never touch Dario Kordic again." And I said, "Go ahead. I don't feel guilty at all, and the least important of all is if you're going to slit my throat." This young man also took out a pistol or a revolver out of his holster a few times, and he knew that inside there was not a bullet, but he would bring it up to my forehead and then he would just trigger this empty gun. He didn't really want to kill me. He just wanted to terrify me by clicking it. It made me feel very uneasy because it was the first time that anyone wanted to slit my throat with a knife. That is a very unpleasant feeling. And another feeling is that somebody puts a gun up by your forehead and tries to trigger it. However, when we moved into the hallway, the entrance door had been broken down and I was facing it with my back, whereas Kordic was facing me, and I don't know if I can say this the way he actually said it. I hope the ladies won't mind. And he said, "Enough of this fucking around," and he fired about 10 centimetres away so the bullet went through the entrance door and went into the yard. I felt very bad.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just pausing there, that was a live bullet? Did it make a noise that your neighbours might have heard?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just "Yes" or "No" to this question. Did that in fact bring out --

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did it bring any help from any of your neighbours?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. After that, a man who heard the shooting thought that they had killed me, and he came down a meadow from the place where he lived to see what had to be done, whether he was supposed to bury me or whether he was supposed to call an ambulance to get me over to the morgue. They thought that I was dead. But they stopped this man. A man with a rifle stopped him and put a rifle at his neck and said, "Franjo, go home and do not interfere in what is going on over here." And this gentleman, Franjo Trogrlic, left my yard and went back home.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Back to the report to the police, I've dealt with the paragraph dealing with the money and the pistol. Then you say that you went -- in the report to the police, you went to get a medical certificate, and you visited the public prosecutor, and you set out how, on the following day, you went to see Kordic and asked him for the money and asked him why he ordered it to be done to you. You set out how your entrance door had been kicked in and how you were beaten and threatened. You attached to that statement a medical certificate, which comes as Exhibit 66.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: This is the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the handwriting is in BCS and hard to read, but the Regional Medical Centre at Zenica recorded on the 1st of April that you were injured by known persons on the 30th of March, having been beaten with fists, rifle butt and wooden pole. Clinically visible contusions on the body, back, both upper and lower arms, and on the fibulas and on the upper legs. Signed by a specialist.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm sorry, this was on the 1st of April?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: The 1st of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, your report to the police was on the 1st of April. Is this the medical certificate you provided to the police or was there another one?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, there is only a referral to hospital, for hospitalisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May the witness now see --

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: However, you omitted a fact here, and that is a grave injury of the brain, contusion and some other injuries, so it's not only --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: (Inaudible)

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we now go to Exhibit 64/2? This is an article that was published and headed, "Cicak beaten and robbed." If the Tribunal goes to the reverse of the second sheet, it will see a photocopy of the very photograph that we've been looking at. Accordingly, if the original is to remain in the court, can it become part of what is 64/3, I think? Alternatively, the Court may decide it's content to work on the basis of both its memory of that original photograph as jogged by this photocopy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I should have thought that was sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Cicak, if you look at the original of this article, only a small part of which has been translated at the moment, can you find a passage, and I think it will be on probably the second or third sheet, where there was some questions asked of you? And I'm going to pick the article up in our summary and part translation, which I'm happy to say on this occasion has French on its reverse side, and goes like this: "Cicak, until recently, a vice-president of the HDZ --" this is a summary of the first part of the article, I think. " -- in Busovaca, although he claims to be in this post even today since his replacement hasn't been carried out according to the rules, came to our offices offering a public statement concerning serious physical attack that he suffered and survived on the 30th of March. He did it in order to show us how he was processed by those who were dissatisfied with the contents of his letters published in," and then newspapers are set out. Now, in the article you were asked, "Mr. Cicak, who were the attackers?" And you set out, a "a young man, 22 or 23, delinquent from Busovaca. I know them all. They are well-armed and trained." You were asked, "Did you anyone inform you in the leadership --" sorry, "Did you inform anyone in the leadership of HDZ in BH of HDZ in BH about the attack?" And you answered, "I did. They offered their sympathy, condemning the extreme wing of the party. I went to see Kordic. He told me that he expected me to come repenting, not complaining. He also said that at the meeting in Grude, Boban reproached him, 'Are you not able to silence that Cicak and his bark?'" . Asked, "Why is it you don't wish to press charges against the attackers?" You answered, "Because this is not a state of law and this is not a civic state." You were asked, "Why did your neighbours not help protect you?" You answered, "What neighbours? They were all hiding." You were asked, "Does that mean that your stand has no support among the Croatian population in the municipality of Busovaca?" And you replied that, "I think that two thirds of these people think as I do, but they are terrified." Now, were those things you were able to say to the press at the time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, yes. There is a bit more, but this is a fair summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you take any part in the political life of Busovaca after the 30th of March, 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did, but not directly. Indirectly, rather.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you stay living where you had lived or not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: I live there until the present day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But did you take any active part in the workings of the party itself?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. No, it was no longer a party.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: After this attack and after your contact in the office with Kordic, did you have any direct personal contact with him again, face-to-face meetings or anything of that sort, or not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In the course of the war, did you serve in any army, and if so, which one and for how long?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: Since I was a military-age man, the relevant municipal authorities of the People's Defence in Zenica called me up and recorded me as a member of the Territorial Defence and later as a member of the BH army. I mean, that was the only legal army at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Cicak, I have a number of questions to complete topics that we've covered in part but which I've omitted to deal with completely, and I'm going to ask you, if you can -- I expect we'll be having a break in about five minutes, but for these questions, I'm going to ask you, if you can, to provide answers that are as short as possible, consistent with giving some clarity to the Chamber. First of all, you've told us about meetings of the officials of the local party. Were the general meetings preceded by private meetings of a limited number of individuals from time to time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: If these were secret meetings, when one thing had to be presented within the narrow circle of the leadership of the party, then yes, but it was supposed to be presented in a milder form to the municipal committee. Then it was reworded and presented in this milder form to the public. That is to say there were two kind of criteria as regards --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you-- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: -- statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you attend these meetings?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: At a few, I did. I attended several dozen or several hundred meetings, and I don't know which one is which any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And where did those secret meetings take place?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: It depended on the nature of the meeting involved. If they were top-secret meetings, then they were held in the premises of the church, or rather this is a part that is called the Sunday school, the old or the new one. First we used the old premises and then we used the new hall for Sunday school, and if there was a meeting where the public could hear about certain things, then it was held in the municipal assembly building in Busovaca, in the hall there; that is to say, in the administrative building itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At meetings, were there ever any -- was there ever any display of a flag or flags?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: You mean as a symbol?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: Believe me, you're asking too much. Well, look, at all events, these flags were flown, and this minute, this second, I cannot remember whether at various meetings where three or four men would meet, or up to six, for example, whether there were flags there already or whether they were put up for that particular occasion. However, as regards every event that was organised, Croatian flags were flown.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were ever anthems played? If so, what anthem or anthems?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: I cannot speak about playing it, because I don't know whether there was an orchestra that knew how to play anything in this village. However, the Croatian anthem was sung, Lijepa Nasa Domovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Finally, on this topic, were any salutes ever used at these meetings? If so, what? And then, can you please show us the salute that was used.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I can. This was a salute dating back to the fascist times of the independent state of Croatia. However, I would need a partner. This salute takes two parts. Do you want me to give you both?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Nice --

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: This is what you do. You raise your hand and you say "Za Dom!" And the other one should say "Spremni!" So it's "Za Dom," and the answer is "Spremni." That was the salute that was used.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was that a salute that had any proper connection with Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: It absolutely had nothing to do whatsoever with Bosnia-Herzegovina. Everything that is related to fascism, to the Ustashas, to the Second World War, has nothing do with Bosnia-Herzegovina except for the fact that the citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina were used for the worst possible objectives.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I want to turn briefly to specialist or paramilitary units. Did such units exist, local specialist or local paramilitary units?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: In Busovaca, a local paramilitary unit was formed. I called it the assault fist, and it was based on the fascist organisation, the Nazi organization in Germany, because the SS units were the assault fist in Germany, too, and it was used to make the disobedient obey. This meant a slow militarisation of the party, that is to say, introducing fascism.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Whose idea was it to create this unit or other units like it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: The idea came from Zagreb, and Mr. Mate Boban had conveyed it. However, the most vociferous proponent of this idea of armed paramilitary formations on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina was Mr. Bozo Rajic. He told us, and we had ample opportunity to see this, that at Kupres, he already had paramilitary units, and he had mistreated Croat, Serb, and Muslim villages and all disobedient persons there. He considered this to be a major success in terms of the organisation of the HDZ party, and he recommended that this be done in Busovaca too. When weapons arrived, this kind of a group was set up in Busovaca, and they were trained, and they practised a lot, and I felt it on my very own back how well they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you say Rajic gave this recommendation, to whom did he make this recommendation in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: Rajic often came to our meetings, and that came as a great surprise to me. How come a mere clerk from the social security company, who had nothing to do with politics, came to our meetings? It was understandable that Mr. Boban came, because he had taken over some of the posts that were to be held by Mr. Tudjman in Bosnia-Herzegovina. He carried out some of his ideas. But Bozo Rajic absolutely had nothing to do with the HDZ. He was a mere clerk, but he was a member of the party, and he was an energetic person, and he developed gradually, and he was aggressive in his statements, and this resulted in the creation of these paramilitary formations at Kupres as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, that would be a convenient moment. We'll adjourn now for 20 minutes. Before we do, let me just deal with some matters of timing this week. We shall be sitting normal hours Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday; Friday is a holiday, so we shall not be sitting. On Thursday we shall have to finish at 12.30. Members of this Chamber have a hearing in the afternoon which is due to begin at 2.00. 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The training of the specialist or paramilitary units to which you've referred, who carried that out? Who organised the training?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: In Busovaca, special training for members of armed forces attached to the HDZ was provided by domestic instructors in backward parts of the mountain, I think it is called Pojila, or something like that, high up -- high above Busovaca. That is where they tried all types of weapons, so that men -- or rather these young men saw a Kalashnikov or M-17 for the first time, and likewise hand-held launchers, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who actually organised the training, or who ran the training?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was run by the municipal HDZ board, and the man responsible was Anto Sliskovic, and Franjo Sliskovic and Igor Prusac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When the decision was made that there should be such training, were you present when that decision was made?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was present at all the meetings which took all sorts of decisions. I cannot remember the date, but when the first armaments arrived that could be used for war purposes, it had to be mastered, or rather men who were to handle those armaments had to acquire some basic knowledge how to use it, but that was not enough, and they were sent on for further training.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did anybody instruct Sliskovic to do the training, or did any body instruct him, or what was the position?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was the HDZ executive board of the municipal board of Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who was in charge of Sliskovic? To whom did Sliskovic answer?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: I mean, if we go back a little, I believe it was the 16th of August or something like that. I don't know. We looked at the document yesterday. Mr. Kordic got the highest military police and civilian powers in the municipality of Busovaca, so he was the only one who could order Sliskovic what to do, how to organise the training, with what men, where, and how much he would be using of ammunition or other materiel.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before I turn to the next short topic, I told the Chamber I would inform them of what "KOS" meant, and it's the counterintelligence service of the former Yugoslavia. That's, as I understand, what it amounts to. I have the B/C/S words, but I imagine it's the English translation that will most assist. If I'm wrong about that, no doubt the Defence can approach me and we'll correct it. I haven't overlooked the fact that I'm going to provide you with a further list of-- a further dramatis personae, supplementary to the one in the pre-trial brief. That will be coming your way, and there are various lists of abbreviations which I can extract and provide for you if you would find such a list helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, you said earlier you would provide a glossary, and it would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'd better get it to you sooner rather than later.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Our next topic, very briefly, you've covered this to some degree already, is the HOS units. You've told us about Kraljevic's death. I'm not sure whether you've covered this single point. After Kraljevic's death, what happened to those men who were in the HOS?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think this question is not all that important. If I may, Your Honours, I should like to add something regarding the training of HDZ members performed at training grounds, if you think it is necessary, if you deem it necessary. If not, then we can go back to this question, but it is up to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Cicak, I think it will be better if you just answer the questions which counsel wants. He has his purpose in asking them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So HOS, what happened to the men after Kraljevic's death? Were they associated with any other group? What else happened to them?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: When Blaz Kraljevic was killed, when he died, his deputy -- I think his name was Anto Prkacin -- disbanded all military units of the HOS a few days later. Some of them were attached to HVO units, those who wanted to, some fled, and those who did not want to were killed. At any rate, Anto Prkacin was the last person who disbanded military units of General Kraljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Two questions about arms dealing. You've told us a bit about the dealing in arms in the territory. Who was the person principally responsible for dealing in arms, if there was a single person who was principally responsible?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: The main person as regards the arming of citizens in that area was Mr. Dario Kordic. Without his knowledge, nothing could be done. So he was the person who decided on every little thing, or on every major thing, too. There were, however, a number of channels by which armaments arrived in the territory of the Lasva Valley. One of those channels went through Herzegovina, across Pavlovica Mountain, and then came down into the Lasva Valley, and the second one came directly from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who benefited most, financially, from the sale of arms in that locality?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: With regard to the financial gain, two men, to my mind, provided for themselves special remuneration. One of them is a professor, we called him "Klempo," in Travnik. I don't know how it will be translated; he has lopsided ears. The money obtained for weapons he kept for himself. The other man who received all the proceeds from armaments was Mr. Dario Kordic. All the receipts, all the bills, went to him. That is, he received all that money. What was the further fate of that money, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've told us something of the movement of the Serbs and of the fact that they had to pay for safe passage. What prices were paid by the Serbs for safe passage?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: This is indeed something which is appalling. Nobody thought that a Croat could take part in such dirty dealings. Mr. Kordic established a bridge with Mr. Radovan Karadzic, a bridge for all those who wanted to leave the territory, beginning from Zenica, that part of Central Bosnia, and who wanted to leave Bosnia and Herzegovina, whether so as not to serve under any army, that is, military formation, or to avoid war and armed conflicts, or be it economic reasons. But the fact is that the convoys from Zenica moved towards Busovaca, and then individuals or groups were then taken on within those convoys by Mr. Kordic, and he took them across the Serb territories to the area of Kobiljaca, and that is where he handed them over to the Serb authorities so they arrived safely to that area. The price per person ranged between 500 marks onward, depending on how much one heard. Some people gave even as much as 1.000 marks to get away, to flee from that area. It doesn't really matter whether they were Bosnians, Muslims, or Croats, or Serbs, or whoever; they all tried to get away from the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. At an earlier stage, you wanted to tell us about Central Bosnian resources of certain types, and I said we'd return to it. Just to fill out the picture of your locality, can you tell us, please, so far as Vitez was concerned, what factory or -- yes, what factory relating to war effort did it have?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: Vitez, or rather the whole of the Lasva Valley up to Bugojno, in those small localities, they were really small places, minor importance after World War II, so in Vitez, an explosives factory was built. In Novi Travnik, an armaments factory was built in Travnik. Military clothes, underwear, and so on and so forth, was made in Bugojno, different parts of armaments, or rather some components. In Vitez, they also made Ekrazit, or rather explosive matter, and large quantities of it were there. And military units, rather the Croatian Defence Council, aspired to lay their hands on those stocks and use them for their own purpose in military combat, and I'm afraid they succeeded in doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of course, in Novi Travnik there was the weapons factory we already know about. In Busovaca, was there anything particularly relevant for the war effort?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was very interesting. That is, the regular authorities in Bosnia-Herzegovina were suspended by Mr. Kordic. Mr. Kordic appropriated the right to cut off a road, any road, to cut it off and block the traffic on that road without asking or without asking for any authorisation to do so. I mean he did it at his own initiative. The reason for that, allegedly, was to prevent Yugoslav, what you call it, army with -- to prevent the Yugoslav army to withdraw some of the armaments from Travnik, which was sheer nonsense, because all that was worth anything in those military factories had been evacuated a long time ago. So that this was simply a show of force, military force, without any authorisation, without any legal foundation, without any legal authorities. It's as if a group of people, for instance, came out here and then blocked the road to Amsterdam and said, "You can't go through."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I cut you short? Did Busovaca have any storage facilities or factory potential that was of significance to the war?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: In Busovaca, there were considerable storage facilities, two of them, in Kaonik and Busovaca itself. Those were very important aircraft parts in Busovaca. It was prepared for military aircraft stationed in Sarajevo, and the repair factory at Rajlovac which was there, and the other part was in Kaonik, where there was an ammunition depot of materiel. But the army had withdrawn it all in due time, so there was nothing left there of importance.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Where was petrol stored, if it was stored in bulk within the area?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, it was at the upper storage facility above Busovaca. Well, in Busovaca, as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. There are three exhibits that I could have dealt with in the chronological series of exhibits that we've already looked at, and I've now just filled them in, although they are out of order. First, please, Exhibit 2701. Just tell us, roughly or precisely, when this photograph was taken, where, and who are the people shown?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: If I begin from my left, first is Bruno Susnja. In the middle is Dario Kordic. To the right is Dragutin Zvonimir Cicak. This photograph was taken on the 21st of March, '91, in Mostar, at the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina convention. You know what a convention is, the congress?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. And --

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think you recognise them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The man Susnja, tell us a bit about him. What was his particular role or function at any time with which we've been concerned?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: At that time, his function was insignificant. Mr. Bruno Susnja is a teacher, and he was engaged in his educational activities at school.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But later --

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: A very nice --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Later, did he get involved in any other activities for the war effort?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes. He became active in a very bad human activity, if I may say so. He procured armaments to kill. He went to various places and brought in various means for killing people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You say that this meeting was on the 21st of March. The Chamber may note that in the chronology, we've got a slightly different date. Are you sure it was the 21st of March or did it run for several days?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't really know. This was taken on the 21st of March, and I remembered it because it should be the first day of spring, if I am correct. That is why I remembered it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At that convention, Kljujic was confirmed as party president. Did Kordic say anything about that to you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: Kordic did not tell me anything about it, whether he was confirmed or not. Kordic was an ordinary delegate there, like all the rest of us. But at that time, there was Mr. Boban was a very interesting and very active -- he was with a group of Herzegovinians who were creating an atmosphere of disorientation, of disorganisation of the convention, itself. And it came as a surprise to all of us who were doing this before that and who knew how to organise things, and we expected that the convention of the Bosnia-Herzegovina HDZ would be at the same level. But when we arrived there, we saw that kind of a conflict was taking place between two currents, and we immediately recognised the Herzegovinian current and the current rallied around Stejpan Kljujic, rather Sarajevo or Central Bosnian, one we did not take part in that conflict at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next exhibit, which is Z13 but not in the core bundle. You have the original before you. You may not have looked at this recently, but I want your help with it, very briefly. It's a document dated the 27th of August of 1991, addressed to the municipal boards of the Croatian Democratic Union, said to be an instruction. And if one looks at the foot of the original and, indeed, the typed English version, there's a stamp but a single signature, namely Kostroman's, after the salutation, "God and the Croats." The body of the document sets out, in paragraph 1, a commentary on the Serbian aggression and expansion policy, makes reference to being at a historic crossroads. Paragraph 2 says that the HDZ BiH presidency, at a session held on the 26th of August of 1991, made a decision to impose a state of emergency which required round-the-clock duties and alertness. Paragraph 3 said that municipal boards shall be closely linked to each other regionally into a unified system of defence, and paragraph 4 are administrative. Were you aware of this signed instruction by Kostroman, ever?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, we were aware of it and I was aware of it, and we considered it, that is, in the light of new developments. What came as a surprise to me is that the secretary general of the HDZ in Bosnia-Herzegovina was nowhere to be found, nor the signature of the president of the Croatian Democratic Community of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that such an important document was signed by a clerk, by an administrative clerk such as Ignac Kostroman. But at that time, we did not look at that signature, even though we found it odd, but we rather riveted our attention on the instruction, what the municipal boards or the Croatian Democratic Union should do in case of the state of emergency. And the result of it was a subsequent decision. Ignac Kostroman had no right to sign such a document, nor distribute it. He did not have the authority for that. But at that time, nobody paid any attention to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: One sees, in the second paragraph of the paragraph number 1, this passage: "The global policies of the HDZ revealed this fastidious policy in our country and abroad so that each day the Croatian people will have a better chance of finally realising their historic aspiration of living in a state of their own, the Republic of Croatia. We are at a historic crossroad and must not make a single mistake that would throw us into the jaws of the Greater Serbia state, which would become a slaughterhouse for Croatian people." Was the expression of the desire to live in the Republic of Croatia or in "a state of their own," was that an accurate reflection of what people were really feeling in August of 1991?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, this is not a correct reflection. You have already seen that it says 140 -- I don't know how many municipal clerks of the HDZ met there, so it was not the Croat people, it was some municipal clerks who met, who had a meeting. Here again we're talking about the aspiration of the Croat people, that is, Bosnian Croats aspiring to join the Croat state. But this is not about Bosnia and Croats aspiring, it is Ignac Kostroman who aspires to adjoin the Croatian state. Not a single Bosnian Croat expects such an aspiration. And even though the HDZ was against, they all voted for an integral Bosnia and Herzegovina at the referendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
