utterances.text: I'm not sure. I think it won its independence later, after attempts to preserve the federal -- that is the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in its rump form, or as some people called it, Serbo-Slavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Right. That was what was left of the former Yugoslavia after the declarations of independence by the countries of Slovenia and Croatia; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you know anything about internal party politics in the HDZ after you left Busovaca at the end of March, 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: I know there were many things, but honestly speaking, I'm not sure. I don't think it was part of an integral Bosnia and Herzegovina, because I think that yesterday or the day before yesterday I said that Bosnia and Herzegovina was divided into three regions, so that is Herzegovina, Central Bosnia, and the Sava Valley. If we're talking about the HDZ in Posavina, in the Sava Valley, then it is a completely different political organisation. The Central Bosnian HDZ is again a different political organisation, and the HDZ in Herzegovina, then again, we need to speak about a completely different organisation. They are territories and regions which are drastically different as far as the mentality, the way of thinking, the way of life, the kind of schools, education, transportation, and in terms of everything or almost everything else, they are different.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. So now to return to the subject that we were discussing, which was the elections in Busovaca, isn't it also true that Dario Kordic was elected secretary of the municipal HDZ in Busovaca on September the 30th, 1990?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: So from the very earliest days of the HDZ in Busovaca, Mr. Kordic was involved in party politics at the local level, just like you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: Not since the earliest days of its existence. First you need to realise that it is a small place, a small village, and after the foundation in the St. Anto's church until the date when we elected the president, vice-president, the secretary, treasurer, and so on and so forth, some time of course elapsed. So this was the time of consultation, of -- I don't know, some personnel development or some personnel structure, rather, the election and selection of people who could be in that organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, over the course of the next year and a half or so, you never actually held a post that was any higher than vice-president of the HDZ at this very basic local municipal level, did you, sir?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I don't know when I was elected to the court of honour, or the disciplinary court, or -- I don't know. I think it was at the HDZ convention in Mostar. I'm not sure whether it was the court of honour of the main board of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina or whether it was the disciplinary commission of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but it is of no consequence to me which bodies these are.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, you've never held the position of president of the municipal HDZ in Busovaca, have you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: There were some proposals, but I did not have the will or desire to become something of that nature, especially not in the village. I didn't think it was necessary, and these efforts within the HDZ and the municipal committee actually filled up part of my free time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, Dario Kordic actually was elected president of the municipal HDZ in Busovaca -- once again, at the local level -- on February the 1st of 1991, was he not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And do you know how long he held that position, sir?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: As president of the municipal committee? I think for a very long period of time. Even after I left, he remained.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you know that Dario Kordic had actually been replaced as president of the municipal HDZ in Busovaca on April the 1st, 1992, by Florijan Glavocevic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: I doubt that. These were replacements. They took place in the context that you are mentioning. If Florijan Glavocevic came, then it was the result of an agreement between Mr. Kordic and Mr. Glavocevic and the others, that is to say, Mate Boban and others. Perhaps Kordic was supposed to take over some higher post, but replacement, no way. The most important person in the Lasva Valley, or rather in that part of Bosnia-Herzegovina, was Dario Kordic. And whatever he says --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I've heard you say that, sir. We've heard that repeatedly this morning. Now, let me just ask you this --

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm glad you heard it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You weren't around in Busovaca in April of 1992, and you have no knowledge of what went on in internal party politics in the HDZ after you left for Zenica on March the 31st of 1992; is that not a fact?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: In April, I lay in my apartment without moving, struggling for my life, to remain alive, throughout the month of April, 1992, because I was beaten up so badly that I couldn't even go to the bathroom, the toilet, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, to answer my question, sir, you had no involvement in internal party politics in the HDZ after March the 31st of 1992; isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think that this is superfluous. I think it's been answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Did you play any part, Mr. Cicak, after the 31st of March?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did play a certain part, in my bed, as I was recovering and trying to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Move on.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: And trying to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've heard that.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: If necessary I'll repeat it ten times.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I don't think that will be necessary, sir. We've heard what you've had to say. Now, the Prosecutor started out looking chronologically at certain documents with you, and the first document that you were shown, chronologically, related to the HDZ. I believe it was dated July the 21st of 1991, and I'll turn to that in just a few seconds, but once again, because these were such tumultuous times in the former Yugoslavia, I would appreciate it if you could just set in historical context for Their Honours what was going on at this time. Do you remember, sir, a famous speech given by President Slobodan Milosevic in March of 1991 in which he declared that Yugoslavia was finished and in which he declared that Serbia no longer considered itself bound by the federal bodies? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I remember those speeches, but I concentrated my attention on the municipal committee of the HDZ of Busovaca and all the affairs related to that. As for Mr. Milosevic's speeches, I wasn't interested in them at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: They didn't concern you in the least?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. And I'm not going to call him "Mr. Milosevic" any more, so I'm going to say that I was never interested in Milosevic's speeches.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, a few days later, President Milosevic announced that Serbs would all live in one state. Did you hear that speech?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Weren't you a little bit scared about that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. Not in the least bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well. Do you remember that a referendum on the question of whether Croatia should become an independent country was held shortly after that, on May the 19th of 1991?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And do you remember, sir, that five months earlier, in December of 1990, a similar kind of referendum had been conducted in Slovenia on the question of whether that country should become independent too?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And do you also remember that shortly before the date of the first document that you were shown, which I believe was marked exhibit Z7, the armed forces of the former Yugoslavia, the JNA, actually attacked Slovenia in a ten-day conflict that lasted, I believe, from June the 25th of 1991 until July the 3rd. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did that make you a little bit worried? Fighting --

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Fighting breaking out in your country? And was that a concern that was shared by your compatriots at the local level of the HDZ party in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know to what level this was developed. At the local level, I know that we discussed this for nights and nights. However, there was a terrible thing that was looming over Bosnia-Herzegovina -- this is also shown by its history -- and that is to say that all the wars in the history of the Balkans started outside the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina and ended so disastrously in Bosnia-Herzegovina that it would be totally devastated. So we were afraid that this war waged between the JNA and Croatia and Slovenia would end in the BH in a disastrous way, that Bosnia-Herzegovina would be devastated and razed to the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And just to close the loop on that question for Their Honours, that was a concern shared by all of your compatriots at the local party level, the HDZ in Busovaca, at around this time, was it not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Because a large quantity -- well, you can't really say a large quantity, but several military formations of the JNA were moving towards Bosnia-Herzegovina, fully armed and equipped, which meant that Bosnia-Herzegovina would be full of weapons of the Yugoslav People's Army, and everybody knows what that can lead to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And certainly the Croat population that you represented in the Opstina of Busovaca knew what that represented, too, didn't they, sir?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: We tried to explain this to the population, because these are people who are not very highly educated and who could not even realise what would happen two months in advance, and we had to make a major effort in order prepare these citizens, but not only those who were of Croat ethnicity but citizens of all different ethnic groups. That is to say that this catastrophe that was looming over Bosnia-Herzegovina posed a constant threat headed by the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. And that brings us to the first document that you were shown, Exhibit Z7. I wonder if the usher would perhaps put that document in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: We've gone over very briefly, and I hope for the Trial Chamber not too laboriously, the historical context out of which these minutes arose, and it's true, is it not, sir, that the reason for the meeting of the Travnik region of the HDZ on the 21st of July of 1991 was to discuss the political and security situation in the homeland?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: On the 21st of July, 1991? The 21st of July, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sure that that meeting was dedicated to that problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: May I add something that you put very nicely? It's good that you raised this question. I don't know if I've answered it, but with the permission of the Honourable Court, I wish to say that that this document was signed by two persons who did not have the right to do so, and that is to say Dario Kordic and Ignac Kostroman. The secretary general, Professor Dr. Markesic is not here at all, or is the president, Stjepan Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, you've previously made that point. Now, Ljubljana, the capital of Slovenia, had actually been bombed by the air forces of the JNA in the middle of July of 1991, or the beginning of July; I'm sorry. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: At this meeting of the HDZ of the Travnik region, Mr. Kljujic was not present, was he?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: He was busy doing other things because he was actually a member of the presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina at this time, was he not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: He was a member of the presidency. He was president of the party, as well. Bosnia-Herzegovina had 110 municipalities, as I said. Perhaps 50 municipalities, or even more, had a Croat population at least in part, and his concern was to strive for each and every Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And the leaders of the seven listed municipalities are identified on this document, are they not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, paragraph 1 of the agenda lists the leaders of all seven municipalities in the Travnik region, and it lists them by name, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. With the permission of the Honourable Court, I would just like to say one sentence: This is an attempt to create two regional communities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: We agreed earlier, at the very outset of this cross-examination, that you were going to answer these questions in a terse, logical, and sequential way, and in a responsive way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Sayers, if the witness does not, it is a matter for the Court to deal with. Now would you move on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The leaders of the seven municipalities are listed accurately in this document, aren't they, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Your name doesn't appear there, does it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know which meeting this was, and it's not important whether my name is there or not. All these minutes were made by Kostroman, and the possibility was always there for some names to be entered and others not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Incidentally, in June of 1991, the Serbian forces had actually launched aggressive attacks into Croatia, had they not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: (No interpreted response)

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, did you say you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I said yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Fine. I'm sorry; I didn't hear you. And you would agree with me this is about one month before the massive Serbian attack on the city of Vukovar in eastern Croatia; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, do you see paragraph 8, sir, of this document?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know. I was given some papers here, and it's very difficult for me to make head or tail out of it. What are these documents? Would you please be so kind as to mark this? Could the usher perhaps help me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Sayers, could we have the document, could we have it put on the ELMO? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: If it's unclear, and I hope it's not, we're discussing Exhibit Z7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Has the witness got Exhibit Z7? Mr. Cicak, would you give to counsel the document that you have. Usher, would you take the document to counsel and see what document it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: This is one of the statements that we earlier questioned him about, Your Honour. It's not relevant to the current line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness have the right document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: If I could just turn your attention to paragraph 8 of these documents, Mr. Cicak, they read that: "For political reasons, the HDZ-BiH must urgently get in touch with the SDA and the other parties in Cazinska Krajina in order to take joint political action in that region." Do you remember -- I think you've previously testified that notwithstanding the absence of your name from the list of attendees, you were actually at this meeting. Did I remember your testimony correctly?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And do you remember a discussion of this particular item, the necessity of a coordinated action with the Muslim political party, the SDA?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: It is interesting to note the Cazinska Krajina and the SDA there, they behaved quite differently from their headquarters, the SDA headquarters in Sarajevo, and that is why the MBO party was interesting and the SDA party was interesting in the Bihac, or rather Cazin region. And that is why this was discussed; that is to say, to try to establish some kind of a link there. But I think it was never established. Nor was it possible to establish it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: But it was certainly the consensus of the meeting and the consensus of all of the attendees that that kind of joint political action with the SDA was something to be advocated and approved of?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: Imperative, if the SDA headquarters in Sarajevo were to be brought down.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And do you remember there being discussion of item 15 on this document, sir, the problem of panic and disorder being spread throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina by armed Chetnik gangs?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And it would be fair to say that the authorities of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina were pretty powerless in controlling that armed violence, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: The authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina were truly powerless in terms of exercising control over all the paramilitary formations that appeared at various sides; Muslim, Croat and Serb paramilitary formations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. And the term "Chetnik" there, I think we've cleared that up. That refers to whom?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know whether they are real Chetniks, but that's the word that was used here. That is to say that it's the only thing that Kostroman wrote down and what he signed. What that means, only Kostroman knows. But they were not Chetnik forces. These were armed formations of the SDS party that, regrettably, we called them Carapani. That is to say, they wore socks, masks, over their faces.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And with this environment of armed violence increasing and the powerlessness of the Bosnian-Herzegovinian governmental authorities to control it, was there any discussion of the item that appears in paragraph 16 about the economy being in a state of general collapse as well?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. This was discussed, and social unrest was almost there. The economy could not function properly. It is very important for the economy to have regular transportation, and there was no regular transportation and traffic because the paramilitary forces placed obstacles and roadblocks, and it was difficult to move about.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you remember any discussion around this time of something called the Brioni Accords?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: Would you please be so kind as to repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Absolutely, sir. Do you remember any discussion around this time of something called the Brioni Accords? And maybe it might help you just to suggest that this was a series of international agreements pursuant to which the declaration of Croatian independence was deferred until about the 8th of November, 1991, to take formal legal effect.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN CICAK (Resumed)
utterances.text: I do not recall these discussions. Right now, I don't know whether we discussed this at the meeting of the municipal committee of the HDZ of Busovaca, but we were very busy dealing with problems that were cropping up then in Busovaca. We wanted to pacify the citizens and also to prepare them for this terrible situation that was looming over Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, if that's a convenient time, we'll adjourn.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Tomorrow at 9.45, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I seek your guidance for a couple of minutes on timetable matters?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's a couple of minutes, no more.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If the witness likes to go, Mr. Cicak, you can go. If you would be back tomorrow at 9.45, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What I'm saying has nothing to do with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, let the witness go. Mr. Cicak, you can go now. This is to do with the hearing, nothing to do with you. Nothing to worry about.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Indeed, it's to do with the timetable of the following witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wonder if we could just ask for the exhibits to be left in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Cicak, could you leave the exhibits, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's a timetable problem. I've been told by Mr. Sayers that he forecasts or did forecast completing cross-examination of this witness within a day, so that would mean that the next witness can start tomorrow at 2.00. I had made arrangements originally to have two witnesses here for this week, but it's quite clear, given that we're rising on Thursday at lunchtime, that we won't finish both of them. So of the two that are in fact here, I've elected to proceed with the one who will take the shorter period of time so that at least he can be completed. Unfortunately, or fortunately, next week I'm obliged to start on Monday at 3.00 with a witness whose timetabling is very difficult, and so I simply have to take him at 3.00, in order that he can be completed and available for other functions that he has to perform within a reasonable period of time. That leaves two possibilities. One is that when the witness finishes this week, if he starts tomorrow at lunchtime, that's Tuesday lunchtime, and if he lasts, say, a day and a bit, sometime Wednesday lunchtime, possibly Wednesday afternoon, there could be some wasted -- not wasted time, some lost time, a maximum of a day, possibly half a day Thursday morning. The other witness who is here, who will be a longer witness in terms of time taken, is willing to stay and is willing to have his evidence started -- it would only be part of his evidence in chief -- on the basis that it goes part heard to however many weeks' time it is. That's not, in itself, a problem because, of course, the transcript will enable us to pick up where he left off, and he can stay out of contact with us once he starts giving his evidence. So I'm really in the Court's hands. My preference, I have to say, is to get evidence in as swiftly and efficiently as we can, but the real options are between a possibility of as much as half a day being lost Thursday morning, the other possibility being a witness, partway through his evidence in chief, coming back in a couple of weeks' time or maybe even a bit more. I have to say the witness has been here before. I had to apologise to him, of course, for the inconvenience he was facing, and he is extremely helpful and cooperative, and he's basically willing to do whatever we say, notwithstanding the fact that he's a doctor himself. So we are grateful to him for that and in your hands as to how best to proceed. But next Monday's witness I have to take at 3.00, when we start.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, we think that we would like to hear the witness, if possible. It rather depends what progress we make.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. s JUDGE MAY: If we don't make good progress and we're faced with him starting, as it were, on Thursday morning, there's little point. But if we can start him on Wednesday afternoon, then I think we should.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll make arrangements, insofar as I can with VWU, to make his return bookings and so on flexible and cancel whatever else. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 4.09 p.m., to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 27th day of April, 1999, at 9.45 a.m. 25
